title: Why Does a Word Go WEIRD When You Repeat It? 🥄
description:
Say "spoon" out loud, fast, over and over. After about thirty goes it stops sounding like a word: the sound is still there, but the meaning drops away. Every time you say it, the sound calls up its meaning, and when the same sound calls it again and again, the link between the two wears out for a while. In 2010 psychologists Xing Tian and David Huber tested where the slowdown happens: not in the word, not in the meaning, but in the connection between them. It's called semantic satiation. In a 2021 study, 94 students copied words like "door" over and over; about 7 in 10 stopped at least once because the word suddenly looked wrong, after about 33 copies. The researchers called it jamais vu, the opposite of déjà vu, and it won the 2023 Ig Nobel Prize for Literature. It wears off in a minute or so. Now try it with your own name. Did the word go weird? Yes or no?
